item.title: Families Turn to Symbolic Cremation After Nepal Floods
item.description:
The funeral pyres at Kathmandu’s riverfront temple have been burning steadily. But instead of bodies, it is effigies they have set ablaze — shaped out of sacred grass, as if to conjure something tangible of the loved ones who disappeared in Nepal’s devastating floods.

Nine days after the walls of mud and debris tore through a Himalayan valley along the border of Nepal and Tibet, wiping out entire towns, the death toll stands at more than 1,200. Relatives of 5,000 others who are missing have searched hospital to hospital, waiting and waiting, hoping for a miracle — or closure at least.

On Friday, rescuers were racing to recover survivors among dozens of people believed to have been found trapped in a tunnel. But to many whose loved ones are among the missing, resignation has begun to set in. According to Hindu rituals in Nepal, the mourning period after a death is 13 days. If the rites are not performed before the 10th day, the clock resets.

Some families, accepting that they may never receive the actual remains, have chosen to perform a symbolic cremation of a figure made of bundles of kusha grass. Nearly 300 effigy cremations have taken place at the temple during the past three days, temple officials said.

Among the solemn onlookers on Thursday at the temple in Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal, was Darshan Bhattarai, 15, who came to carry out the last rites for his father, Pushpa Raj Bhattarai, 46, one of the thousands dead or missing.

Darshan had been living in the city with his mother, Kamala, and attending a private school thanks to the salary earned by his father, about $300 a month, relatives said. In search of a better life, the family had first moved from Nepal’s eastern hills to the southern plains, where Mr. Bhattarai for years ran a retail shop. About a decade ago, he got a job as an administrative assistant in Nepal’s hydropower sector. He was posted in one of the projects in Trishuli, an area devastated by the floods last week.

Nepal’s hydroelectric projects experienced some of the worst damage from the floods, caused by a glacial collapse that cascaded into an overwhelming rush of mud, gravel and water. Some workers were swept away. Others were trapped in tunnels. Teams of rescue workers have spent days trying to find a way in.

“When his phone went off, we knew something was wrong,” Sukhdev Khanal, a relative of Mr. Bhattarai’s, said. “One of his colleagues had gone out for a smoke, and he survived. He told us later that the rest were swept away.”

After a week of no news, hope dimmed. So Mr. Bhattarai’s family came to the temple in Kathmandu, Pashupatinath Temple, before the 10th day passed, to perform the cremation on the banks of the Bagmati River.

Darshan arrived with his mother and other family and friends. The priest, Rishi Neupane, came with the necessary items for the cremation: kusha grass, kindling wood, rice, ghee and marigolds. A piece of cloth to serve as a shroud. Darshan and his family watched as Mr. Neupune twisted and bound bundles of the grass until it resembled a large straw doll.

As is customary, Darshan’s head had to be shaved as an act of purification before he could perform the ceremony.

He went to a tap on the side of the temple, ran his head under the water and sat on the edge of stair, as a neighbor used a razor and began shaving lock after lock. Darshan giggled as one of his young cousins felt his shaved head, caressing the tuft of hair that is usually left at the crown, a tender moment before the ceremony.

Then, the priest began his work, laying a printed photo of Mr. Bhattarai on a bamboo stretcher and placing the effigy on top.

Through two hours of rituals, Darshan’s face was blank, even when the rain started lashing. Darshan and some of the relatives pulled back, seeking refuge under a ledge, as the priest, and half a dozen men continued. Mr. Bhattarai’s sister-in-law, umbrella in hand, made a video call to his elderly parents in the village, showing them the effigy.

As the rain poured down, Darshan and the men lowered the effigy into the river, for a cleansing bath, as people took turns paying respects to the photo of Mr. Bhattarai.

Praveen Bhattarai, 40, a childhood friend of Mr. Bhattarai’s, was among the mourners. He said he had last seen him during a visit home for the Dussehra festival last year. They had played cards. Mr. Bhattarai was someone who always kept the mood light, he said.

“Doing the last rites like this is very difficult for the family,” Praveen Bhattarai said. “Somewhere, in the depth of their heart, the question will always be there — that maybe he is alive.”

The family lifted the stretcher and walked in a procession, through the thick smoke of other burning pyres, crossing a bridge over the river to the stone platform where Mr. Bhattarai’s pyre would be set.

Darshan lit the fire.

As his uncle steadied him from behind, the young man walked around the effigy as it burned, followed by his mother. They watched it turn to ash, and then Darshan stepped down to submerge some of the ashes in the river.

As the priest read a final prayer from his mobile phone, the family and friends used water from the river to purify the platform where the cremation had taken place.

Mother and son, with relatives holding their arms, slowly made their way through the temple grounds. As they exited, they passed a large group of pilgrims — dancing to drums, singing “Om namah Shiva!” in praise of the god whose spiritual home is nearby.

They kept going, with Darshan almost being pulled by his uncle, as if sleepwalking into a heavy future.

item.title: Here Is Where Ukraine Peace Talks Stand, as a New Round Approaches
item.description:
Trump administration envoys arrived on Saturday in Moscow in an effort to restart talks to end the war between Russia and Ukraine, over six months after a previous round of discussions fizzled out.

The trip by Steve Witkoff, the administration’s peace envoy, and Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, came even as Russian and Ukrainian forces are locked in an escalating spiral of airstrikes.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Thursday that U.S. envoys would “have a meeting in Moscow and another one in Kyiv,” Ukraine’s capital. He added: “It is important that America remain actively engaged. We are ready to meet with them in Ukraine — properly and substantively.”

Kyrylo Budanov, the Ukrainian delegation’s leader at the previous talks, told The New York Times in a recent interview that negotiations mediated by the Trump administration were expected to begin by late September, days after Russia’s parliamentary election and weeks before U.S. midterm elections.

It is not clear whether a new round of talks will yield more progress than previous ones. But “negotiations will sooner or later come to something,” Mr. Budanov told The Times. “You cannot fight your whole life.”

Here is what to know about peace talks and where they stand.

Russia and Ukraine have been talking at various levels since February 2022, when Russian forces mounted a full-scale invasion of Ukrainian territory. Despite brief cease-fires and occasional prisoner swaps, the two sides have made little headway toward ending the war.

A new flurry of high-level, U.S.-brokered negotiations began shortly after Mr. Trump — who claimed he could end the war in a day — took office in January 2025.

The last round of face-to-face talks was held in February, when Ukrainian and Russian negotiators met in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, and then later in Geneva. But there was no breakthrough in those discussions, and they ground to a halt after the United States and Israel went to war against Iran, a conflict that has consumed the Trump administration’s attention.

Since then, there have been limited contacts between Moscow and Kyiv, but the major issues have remained on hold.

In June, Mr. Zelensky published an open letter to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia that offered to resume peace talks, but that also taunted the Russian leader. Mr. Putin, who has shown little serious interest in peace negotiations, recently pledged to pursue the war.

The last round of negotiations focused a 20-point peace plan that covered a broad range of issues, including security guarantees that Ukraine seeks to prevent future Russian aggression, and commitments to rebuild the war-ravaged nation.

But the two sides have struggled to reach common ground on several crucial points, including the possible deployment of Western forces in Ukraine, control of territory in the country’s east, and management of a Russian-occupied nuclear power plant.

Russia has demanded that Ukraine hand over the land it controls in the eastern Donetsk region as a condition for ending the war, a strip of territory about 50 miles long and 40 miles wide that includes dozens of towns and villages. Ukraine has refused to withdraw unilaterally, arguing that ceding land would embolden Russia to attack again, and it has asked for guarantees that would deter Moscow from violating any cease-fire.

The United States has been the main mediator in talks between Russia and Ukraine.

But European leaders — nervous that Mr. Trump will cut them out of any settlement — are trying to take a more active role in ending the war, whose outcome could shape the continent’s security for decades to come. Mr. Trump has also made it clear that he sees Ukraine as a European responsibility.

European diplomats are working on a format for future negotiations to protect European interests that would be led by France, Germany and Britain, European officials said last month.

The front, stretching hundreds of miles through eastern Ukraine, has largely been frozen. The terrain has been devastated, a killing field dominated by drones, making troop movement a lethal risk.

As a result, Russia and Ukraine have instead intensified a campaign of airstrikes that have caused death and destruction in cities far from the battlefield. Over the summer, the two sides have launched drones and missiles at energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and ports that are crucial to grain exports.

Note: As of Aug. 3. Includes Ukrainian drone and missile attacks inside Russia. Strikes within 60 miles of the border are not shown. Source: Armed Conflict Location & Event Data. The New York Times

Russia has pummeled Kyiv with unrelenting daytime attacks of new jet-powered drones, taking advantage of a Ukrainian shortage of air defenses. Ukraine has launched attacks increasingly deep into Russia’s territory, disrupting its economy and isolating Crimea.

Even if negotiations resume this month, conditions for a cease-fire are unlikely to come until spring, Mr. Budanov told The Times. Russia is expected to attempt to break Ukraine in another strategic winter bombing campaign, the fourth of the war.

More than two million Russian and Ukrainian troops have been killed or wounded in the four years that Russia has been waging war against its neighbor, according to one study.
